Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

i'm sending this update about the ticket exchange for Mara Velez's trip from Bellford to North Quay on 18 October. she bought the 08:42 service through the station desk on 3 October, and the printed ticket shows carriage C, seat 18. on Monday she came back because a family appointment had moved and she wanted to travel on the 10:16 instead. she asked whether the exchange could be handled at the desk without cancelling the whole booking. the appointment was the reason she gave, but she didn't ask for any refund, and nobody at the counter told her that one was due.

The 10:16 service was listed as running from Bellford to North Quay with one change at Westmere. The original 08:42 service was direct. Mara said that the change was acceptable as long as the Westmere connection left enough time to get from platform 2 to platform 5. She had a small suitcase and said she could use the stairs, but did not want to rely on a lift. The desk agent looked at the timetable sheet that was beside the till and said the printed connection time was 14 minutes. Mara asked if the 10:16 ticket would include a seat for both parts of the journey, rather than just the first train.

1. What the counter record shows: the agent put the original ticket beside the keyboard and checked the exchange screen at 09:11. The screen showed a fare difference of £6.40, and a service fee of £8.00. Mara paid by card; the terminal slip has the time 09:16 and the last four digits 4472. The desk kept the original paper ticket, then printed a new itinerary and two seat coupons. The itinerary lists carriage D, seat 22 from Bellford to Westmere, and carriage A, seat 11 from Westmere to North Quay. The agent wrote the exchange reference, BX-7316, on the top right corner of the itinerary. Mara checked the dates and destination before leaving, but she did not check the carriage letters against the platform display.

At 09:24 she came back to the same counter. She said the new itinerary had the right date but she was unsure whether the Westmere transfer involved crossing the footbridge, and she wanted to know if there was a route that avoided it. The agent looked at a station map in the desk folder. On that map, the accessible route between platforms 2 and 5 goes through the concourse and uses a ramp, rather than the footbridge. The map did not give a walking time. The agent told Mara, “The connection is shown as fourteen minutes, but I can't tell you how busy the concourse will be.” Mara said she understood and kept the exchange rather than asking for a different train. This was not a confirmation that the transfer would be easy for her, only the information the desk had available then.

The two seat coupons have separate reservation numbers. The first is 593814 for the Bellford–Westmere leg, and the second is 593901 for Westmere–North Quay. Both are dated 18 October. The itinerary gives the arrival at Westmere as 11:02 and departure as 11:16. A handwritten note on the desk copy says “platforms subject to change”; there is no platform number printed on Mara's ticket. The desk agent said platform numbers would be on the station boards on the day, and Mara asked whether she should check those boards before going to the first platform. The agent said yes. No one checked the live service information during the exchange, because the travel date was still several days away.

2. The remaining documents and messages: Mara kept the card slip, itinerary, and both seat coupons in one envelope. She emailed a photograph of them to the travel office on Tuesday morning, asking the office to confirm that the two coupons covered the whole route. The email did not ask the office to change the booking, and it did not say that the exchange had failed. The travel office has not replied in the record available to me. A note from the ticket desk says the original ticket was retained with the daily exchange paperwork, but the note does not say whether a scan was made. The printed itinerary lists the fare difference and service fee separately; it does not explain how either amount was calculated.

Mara also said she had first considered moving the trip to 19 October, but the family appointment was on the evening of the 18th and she needed to arrive in North Quay that day. She did not ask to alter the destination or add another passenger. Her request at the counter was to exchange the 08:42 booking for the 10:16 itinerary on the same date, and her later question was specifically about the transfer route and whether both legs had reserved seats. The desk record does not show that she asked for assistance at Westmere, or that assistance was booked.

My assessment is limited to the exchange paperwork and the information recorded at the desk. Those records show a new itinerary for 18 October with two reserved seats and a 14-minute connection at Westmere, but they do not establish the platform that will be used, the crowding or walking conditions on the day, or whether Mara will be able to make the transfer comfortably. The accessible route shown on the map avoids the footbridge, although no walking time is stated. If the station boards show a different platform arrangement on 18 October, the route information may not describe the transfer she actually needs to make.
